source: However, CEM-GXR cells either co-cultured with MAIT cells or separated in transwell plates showed no suppression of HIV-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) suggesting that direct cell contact is not necessary for the MAIT-derived inhibition of HIV-1 infection (Figure 3—source data 1).

claim: IL-12/18-stimulated MAIT cells upregulated production of the antiviral chemokine MIP-1β (CCL4).
source: Interestingly, IL-12/18-stimulated MAIT cells also upregulated production of the antiviral chemokine MIP-1β (CCL4) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experimental data, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: CCL4 is a ligand for the HIV-1 entry receptor CCR5.
source: This chemokine is a ligand for the HIV-1 entry receptor CCR5 and hence can restrict HIV-1 infection by blocking viral entry.
evidence: This is a statement about CCL4 function based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: CCL4 can restrict HIV-1 infection by blocking viral entry.
source: This chemokine is a ligand for the HIV-1 entry receptor CCR5 and hence can restrict HIV-1 infection by blocking viral entry.
evidence: This is a statement about CCL4 function based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Higher levels of CCL4 were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (p = 0.125).
source: Higher levels of all three chemokines were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (CCL4 p = 0.125, CCL3 p = 0.0156, CCL5 p = 0.0078), although these differences were not statistically significant for CCL4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's ELISA data.

claim: Higher levels of CCL3 were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (p = 0.0156).
source: Higher levels of all three chemokines were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (CCL4 p = 0.125, CCL3 p = 0.0156, CCL5 p = 0.0078), although these differences were not statistically significant for CCL4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's CBA data with statistical significance.

claim: Higher levels of CCL5 were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (p = 0.0078).
source: Higher levels of all three chemokines were expressed by stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (CCL4 p = 0.125, CCL3 p = 0.0156, CCL5 p = 0.0078), although these differences were not statistically significant for CCL4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's CBA data with statistical significance.

claim: There was a significant increase in CCL4 expression in IL-12/18 stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (p = 0.0169).
source: Although only CCL4 was detectable by this method, the results showed a significant increase in CCL4 expression in IL-12/18 stimulated MAIT cells compared to the unstimulated controls (p = 0.0169) confirming data from the stimulated MAIT supernatants (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's flow cytometry data with statistical significance.

claim: CD161++ Vα7.2+ cells are highly enriched within the CCL4-producing subset, accounting on average for 60% of this population.
source: Further, gating on all CCL4+ cells within the total CD8+ T cells, revealed that CD161++ Vα7.2+ cells are highly enriched within the CCL4-producing subset (Figure 4D), accounting on average for 60% of this population.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's flow cytometry data, with reference to a figure.

claim: MAIT cells likely represent the major source of CCL4 in the model system.
source: Hence, MAIT cells likely represent the major source of CCL4 in our model system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the flow cytometry data showing MAIT cell enrichment in CCL4+ cells.

claim: MAIT cells are capable of producing CXCL12/SDF-1, the ligand for the alternative HIV-1 entry co-receptor, CXCR4.
source: Subsequent profiling of the effector molecules produced by MAITs showed that they are also capable of producing CXCL12/SDF-1, the ligand for the alternative HIV-1 entry co-receptor, CXCR4.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experimental data.

claim: CXCL12 induction required TCR signaling, as it was only observed in co-culture of MAIT cells with 5-OP-RU-loaded THP-1 cells.
source: In contrast to CCL3, 4 and 5, CXCL12 induction required TCR signaling, as it was only observed in co-culture of MAIT cells with 5-OP-RU-loaded THP-1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experimental data, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: No anti-HIV-1 effect of IL-12/18-stimulated supernatants was observed when the CXCR4 tropic HIV-1LAI virus was used instead of HIVBAL.
source: In accordance with these results, no anti-HIV-1 effect of IL-12/18-stimulated supernatants was observed when the CXCR4 tropic HIV-1LAI virus was used instead of HIVBAL to infect the target cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro infection assay, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Upon IL12/18 stimulation MAIT cells significantly increase expression of known HIV-1 restriction factors.
source: Therefore, upon IL12/18 stimulation MAIT cells significantly increase expression of known HIV-1 restriction factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on chemokine production.

claim: The addition of blocking antibodies to CCL3/4/5 neutralized the inhibitory effect of the IL12/18-stimulated supernatant and restored GFP expression to levels equivalent to the control condition.
source: Strikingly, the addition of these blocking antibodies neutralized the inhibitory effect of the IL12/18-stimulated supernatant and restored GFP expression to levels equivalent to the control condition (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro infection assay with blocking antibodies, with reference to a figure.

claim: The anti-viral activity of MAIT cells in relation to HIV-1 is mediated at least in part by expression of the chemokines CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5.
source: Taken together these data indicate that the anti-viral activity of MAIT cells in relation to HIV-1 is mediated at least in part by expression of the chemokines CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the blocking antibody experiments.

claim: Depletion of MAIT cells in blood of HIV-1-infected individuals has been subsequently broadly confirmed with effects seen in acute, chronic and long-term treated infection.
source: The impact of HIV-1 on MAIT cell populations was initially noted by two groups in 2012, and depletion of MAIT cells in blood of HIV-1-infected individuals has been subsequently broadly confirmed with effects seen in acute, chronic and long-term treated infection, and reproduced here (Eberhard et al., 2016; Cosgrove et al., 2013; Spaan et al., 2016; Paquin-Proulx et al., 2017; Leeansyah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell depletion in HIV-1 infection supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Viruses can activate MAIT cells efficiently in vivo.
source: Given recent data indicating that viruses can activate MAIT cells efficiently in vivo (van Wilgenburg et al., 2016) and provide protection against lethal challenge in a mouse model (van Wilgenburg et al., 2018), we aimed to define whether MAIT cells can respond to and suppress HIV-1.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell activation by viruses supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MAIT cells provide protection against lethal challenge in a mouse model.
source: Given recent data indicating that viruses can activate MAIT cells efficiently in vivo (van Wilgenburg et al., 2016) and provide protection against lethal challenge in a mouse model (van Wilgenburg et al., 2018), we aimed to define whether MAIT cells can respond to and suppress HIV-1.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell function in a mouse model supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Granzyme B-positive MAIT cells were detected during acute HIV-1 infection (PHI), up to 10-fold higher than HIV-1- controls.
source: Granzyme B-positive MAIT cells were detected during acute HIV-1 infection (PHI), up to 10-fold higher than HIV-1- controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: During chronic infection the majority of MAIT cells were granzyme B+, more than 90% for some individuals.
source: During chronic infection the majority of MAIT cells were granzyme B+, more than 90% for some individuals.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The granzyme B expression pattern in MAIT cells during HIV-1 infection is highly congruent with those seen during acute dengue and influenza infections.
source: These data are highly congruent with those seen during acute dengue and influenza infections (Loh et al., 2016; van Wilgenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature on MAIT cell activation in other viral infections.

claim: Residual MAIT cells in chronic HCV-infection showed an activated phenotype with high levels of granzyme B, HLA-DR, PD-1 and CD69 expression.
source: Residual MAIT cells in chronic HCV-infection showed an activated phenotype with high levels of granzyme B, HLA-DR, PD-1 and CD69 expression (Hengst et al., 2016) and granzyme B levels remain high after successful cure (van Wilgenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell phenotype in HCV infection supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Granzyme B levels in MAIT cells remain high after successful HCV cure.
source: Residual MAIT cells in chronic HCV-infection showed an activated phenotype with high levels of granzyme B, HLA-DR, PD-1 and CD69 expression (Hengst et al., 2016) and granzyme B levels remain high after successful cure (van Wilgenburg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell phenotype after HCV cure supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MAIT cells were not reinvigorated following HCV clearance and remained dysfunctional.
source: MAIT cells were not reinvigorated following HCV clearance and remained dysfunctional (Hengst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell function after HCV clearance supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sustained expression of granzyme B and PD-1 was observed during tuberculosis (TB) and HIV-1/TB co-infection.
source: Sustained expression of granzyme B and PD-1 was also observed during tuberculosis (TB) and HIV-1/TB co-infection (Jiang et al., 2014; Saeidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell phenotype in TB infection supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blockade of PD-1 on MAIT cells during TB infection resulted in significantly higher IFNγ expression when stimulated with BCG.
source: Blockade of PD-1 on MAIT cells during TB infection resulted in significantly higher IFNγ expression when stimulated with BCG.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell function in TB infection, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: MAIT cells migrate toward mucosal sites, recognise bacterial metabolites and contribute to barrier immunity.
source: MAIT cells are known to migrate toward mucosal sites, recognise bacterial metabolites and contribute to barrier immunity (Voillet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell function supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MAIT cell frequencies in rectal tissue of treated PHI donors were not found to be substantially different from HIV-1- controls.
source: MAIT cell frequencies in rectal tissue of treated PHI donors were not found to be substantially different from HIV-1- controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Higher percentages of MAIT cells were found within the rectum of HIV-1+ individuals, compared to terminal ileum.
source: In this study, higher percentages were found within the rectum of HIV-1+ individuals, compared to terminal ileum.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: In pigtail macaques, MAIT cells exhibited lower expression of the gut homing marker α4β7 and were not enriched in the gut prior to SIV infection.
source: In pigtail macaques, MAIT cells exhibited lower expression of the gut homing marker α4β7 and were not enriched in the gut prior to SIV infection.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cells in pigtail macaques, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Following SIV infection in pigtail macaques, MAIT cells upregulated α4β7 and their frequencies increased within the rectum.
source: Following infection, they upregulated α4β7 and their frequencies increased within the rectum (Juno et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cells in pigtail macaques supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Upregulation of α4β7 and increased MAIT cell frequencies in the rectum following SIV infection may prevent depletion of MAIT cells during chronic infection.
source: The authors postulated that this may prevent depletion of MAIT cells during chronic infection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement from previous literature.

claim: There is a general reduction of MAIT cells in both blood and tissue compartments during HIV-1 infection.
source: This suggests that there is a general reduction of MAIT cells in both compartments.

source: The THP-1 monocytic cell line was used as it has been extensively trialled by our group and many others as an effective APC for MAIT cells in microbial and viral infections (Ussher et al., 2018; van Wilgenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the THP-1 cell line supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: THP1 sensing of HIV-1BAL may be through TLR7/8 or cytosolic RIG-like receptors.
source: THP1 sensing of HIV-1BAL may be through TLR7/8 or cytosolic RIG-like receptors (Diget et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014), which in turn activate THP-1 cells to secrete inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-18 (Bandera et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of THP-1 activation, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: THP-1 cells activated by HIV-1BAL secrete inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-18.
source: THP1 sensing of HIV-1BAL may be through TLR7/8 or cytosolic RIG-like receptors (Diget et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2014), which in turn activate THP-1 cells to secrete inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-18 (Bandera et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about THP-1 cell function supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Inactivated virus was incapable of activating THP-1 cells.
source: Inactivated virus was incapable of activating THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experimental data.

claim: Cross-linking of nucleocapsid P7 protein by aldrithiol-2 may not allow single stranded HIV-1 RNA within virions to bind to TLR7/8.
source: This could be due to the cross-linking of nucleocapsid P7 protein by aldrithiol-2, which may not allow single stranded HIV-1 RNA within virions to bind to TLR7/8 (Rossio et al., 1998).

claim: Inactivation of influenza and HCV also impacted on MAIT cell recognition in vitro.
source: We note that inactivation of influenza and HCV also impacted on MAIT cell recognition in vitro (van Wilgenburg et al., 2018), even in a macrophage culture where true infection and replication does not occur.

claim: IFN-γ production dependent on IL-12 and IL-18 has been observed in other infection models.

evidence: This is a statement about IFN-γ production supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stimulation of MAIT cells by IL-12 and IL-18 activates the cells independent of TCR signalling to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and cytotoxic granules.
source: It must be noted that stimulation of MAIT cells by IL-12 and IL-18 not only activates the cells independent of TCR signalling to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and cytotoxic granules, but it also increases caspase-3 expression, a pro-apoptotic marker.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell activation mechanisms, drawing from the study's data and established knowledge.

claim: Stimulation of MAIT cells by IL-12 and IL-18 increases caspase-3 expression, a pro-apoptotic marker.
source: It must be noted that stimulation of MAIT cells by IL-12 and IL-18 not only activates the cells independent of TCR signalling to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and cytotoxic granules, but it also increases caspase-3 expression, a pro-apoptotic marker.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: IL-12 can induce apoptosis of CD8+ T cells in the absence of antigenic stimulation.
source: It has been shown that IL-12 can induce apoptosis of CD8+ T cells in the absence of antigenic stimulation (Fan et al., 2002) and it has also been observed that MAIT cells show PLZF-dependent enhanced capacity for apoptotic death following stimulation (Gérart et al., 2013).

claim: MAIT cells show PLZF-dependent enhanced capacity for apoptotic death following stimulation.
source: It has been shown that IL-12 can induce apoptosis of CD8+ T cells in the absence of antigenic stimulation (Fan et al., 2002) and it has also been observed that MAIT cells show PLZF-dependent enhanced capacity for apoptotic death following stimulation (Gérart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell apoptosis supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overall HIV-1-induced depletion of MAITs could very likely be due to activation induced apoptosis.
source: Overall HIV-1-induced depletion of MAITs could very likely be due to activation induced apoptosis, as observed in other disease settings (Wakao et al., 2017; Hinks, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the mechanism of MAIT cell depletion, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MAIT cells can produce a broad range of factors following stimulation.
source: Both MAIT cells and THP-1 cells can produce a broad range of factors following stimulation as has been recently described (Hinks et al., 2019; Lamichhane et al., 2020; Leng et al., 2019).

claim: Original in vitro studies revealed no antiviral effect of IFNγ and even enhancement of infection in primary cells.
source: This is consistent with original in vitro studies which revealed no antiviral effect of IFNγ and even enhancement of infection in primary cells (Yamamoto et al., 1986; Mackewicz et al., 1994) and several clinical trials that revealed no impact of this cytokine in vivo (Roff et al., 2014).

claim: Several clinical trials revealed no impact of IFNγ in vivo in HIV-1 infection.
source: This is consistent with original in vitro studies which revealed no antiviral effect of IFNγ and even enhancement of infection in primary cells (Yamamoto et al., 1986; Mackewicz et al., 1994) and several clinical trials that revealed no impact of this cytokine in vivo (Roff et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about IFNγ function in HIV-1 infection supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CCR5 levels play an important role in the long-term outcome of HIV-1 infection.
source: Even in the absence of killing it is clearly evident that CCR5 levels play an important role in the long-term outcome of HIV-1 infection (McLaren et al., 2015) and thus this effect could certainly contribute to control of HIV-1 levels in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about CCR5 function in HIV-1 infection supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MAIT cell-mediated CCR5 blockade could contribute to control of HIV-1 levels in vivo.
source: Even in the absence of killing it is clearly evident that CCR5 levels play an important role in the long-term outcome of HIV-1 infection (McLaren et al., 2015) and thus this effect could certainly contribute to control of HIV-1 levels in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the potential impact of MAIT cells on HIV-1 control.

claim: MAIT cells are present in relevant tissues in persistent HIV-1 infection, including under therapy.
source: More intriguingly, since MAIT cells are present in relevant tissues in persistent infection, including under therapy, it will be important to consider their role in strategies for cure.
evidence: This is a statement about MAIT cell distribution, drawing from the study's data and established knowledge.
